Analogous to scalar ordinary differential equations (ODEs), the Wronskian of vector-valued functions can be used to determine linear dependency. In particular:

items.readable_text:
Content:
A pair of solutions [MATH: \mathbf{x}_1(t)] and [MATH: \mathbf{x}_2(t)] to a [MATH: 2\times 2] homogeneous linear system
[MATH: \mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)]
is called a fundamental set of solutions on an interval if the solutions are linearly independent on that interval.

Content:
A practical test for determining whether a pair of functions forms a fundamental set of solutions is to use the Wronskian:

Content:
> If [MATH: \mathbf{x}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{x}_2] are solutions to the system and
> [MATH: W(\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2) \neq 0]
> for at least one [MATH: t_0] in the interval, then they form a fundamental set of solutions on that interval.

Content:
This definition generalizes to any [MATH: n\times n] homogeneous linear system [MATH: \mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t).] A set of solutions
[MATH: \mathbf{x}_1(t),\ \mathbf{x}_2(t),\ \ldots,\ \mathbf{x}_n(t)]
is a fundamental set of solutions on an interval if the solutions are linearly independent on that interval.

Content:
The same Wronskian idea applies: compute the determinant of the [MATH: n\times n] matrix whose columns are [MATH: \mathbf{x}_1(t),\ldots,\mathbf{x}_n(t).] If it is nonzero at some [MATH: t_0] in the interval, then the solutions form a fundamental set on that interval.

Content:
Next, we will look at a concrete example applying this test.

  1. The function [MATH: [t^{2} + 1; − 4t]] is a solution of the system.

  2. The function [MATH: [2t + 1; − 4t]] is a solution of the system.

  3. The function [MATH: [t; 1 − 2t]] is a solution of the system.

Also, determine which pair of solutions forms a set of fundamental solutions to the system.

[MATH: {x_{1}^{′}(t) = 2x_{1}(t) + x_{2}(t); x_{2}^{′}(t) = − 4x_{1}(t) − 2x_{2}(t).]
Consider the system of linear ODEs above, where [MATH: t\in\mathbb R.] Which of the following statements are true?

1. The function [MATH: [t^{2} + 1; − 4t]] is a solution of the system.
2. The function [MATH: [2t + 1; − 4t]] is a solution of the system.
3. The function [MATH: [t; 1 − 2t]] is a solution of the system.

Also, determine which pair of solutions forms a set of fundamental solutions to the system.

sections.normalized_html:
The Wronskian [MATH: W(\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2)] of two vector-valued functions [MATH: [x_{11}(t); x_{21}(t)]] is defined as [MATH: |x_{11}(t)|x_{12}(t); x_{21}(t)|x_{22}(t)|]

Note the following:

  • If the Wronskian is not identically zero, then [MATH: \mathbf{x}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{x}_2] are linearly independent.

  • If the Wronskian is identically zero, and it's known that [MATH: \mathbf{x}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{x}_2] are solutions to the same system of linear ODEs, then [MATH: \mathbf{x}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{x}_2] are linearly dependent.

First, we write our system in matrix form:

[MATH: [2|1; − 4|− 2]]

Now, let's substitute the given vectors into the matrix differential equation:

  • [MATH: [t^{2} + 1; − 4t]] [MATH: \text{isn't}] a solution of the system. Indeed: [MATH: [(t^{2} + 1)^{′}; (− 4t)^{′}]|= [2|1; − 4|− 2][t^{2} + 1; − 4t]; [2t; − 4]|= [2 ⋅ (t^{2} + 1) + 1 ⋅ (− 4t); − 4 ⋅ (t^{2} + 1) + (− 2) ⋅ (− 4t)]; [2t; − 4]|= [2t^{2} − 4t + 2; − 4t^{2} + 8t − 4]×]

  • [MATH: [2t + 1; − 4t]] [MATH: \text{is}] a solution of the system. Indeed: [MATH: [(2t + 1)^{′}; (− 4t)^{′}]|= [2|1; − 4|− 2][2t + 1; − 4t]; [2; − 4]|= [2 ⋅ (2t + 1) + 1 ⋅ (− 4t); − 4 ⋅ (2t + 1) + (− 2) ⋅ (− 4t)]; [2; − 4]|= [2; − 4]✓]

  • [MATH: [t; 1 − 2t]] [MATH: \text{is}] a solution of the system. Indeed: [MATH: [(t)^{′}; (1 − 2t)^{′}]|= [2|1; − 4|− 2][t; 1 − 2t]; [1; − 2]|= [2 ⋅ t + 1 ⋅ (1 − 2t); − 4 ⋅ t + (− 2) ⋅ (1 − 2t)]; [1; − 2]|= [1; − 2]✓]

Now, consider the set of solutions [MATH: \big\{ \mathbf{b},\mathbf{c} \big\}.] Its Wronskian is

[MATH: W(b, c)|=|2t + 1|t; − 4t|1 − 2t|; = (2t + 1) ⋅ (1 − 2t) − t ⋅ (− 4t); = (2t + 1)(1 − 2t) + 4t^{2}; = 1]

which is nonzero for at least one [MATH: t \in \mathbb R.] Thus, since [MATH: \mathbf b] and [MATH: \mathbf c] are both solutions of the same linear system, and their Wronskian is nonzero for at least one [MATH: t\in\mathbb R,] [MATH: \big\{ \mathbf{b},\mathbf{c} \big\}] is a set of fundamental solutions of the system.
sections.readable_text:
The Wronskian [MATH: W(\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2)] of two vector-valued functions
[MATH: [x_{11}(t); x_{21}(t)]]
is defined as
[MATH: |x_{11}(t)|x_{12}(t); x_{21}(t)|x_{22}(t)|]

Note the following:

- If the Wronskian is not identically zero, then [MATH: \mathbf{x}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{x}_2] are linearly independent.
- If the Wronskian is identically zero, and it's known that [MATH: \mathbf{x}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{x}_2] are solutions to the same system of linear ODEs, then [MATH: \mathbf{x}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{x}_2] are linearly dependent.

First, we write our system in matrix form:

[MATH: [2|1; − 4|− 2]]

Now, let's substitute the given vectors into the matrix differential equation:

- [MATH: [t^{2} + 1; − 4t]] [MATH: \text{isn't}] a solution of the system. Indeed:
[MATH: [(t^{2} + 1)^{′}; (− 4t)^{′}]|= [2|1; − 4|− 2][t^{2} + 1; − 4t]; [2t; − 4]|= [2 ⋅ (t^{2} + 1) + 1 ⋅ (− 4t); − 4 ⋅ (t^{2} + 1) + (− 2) ⋅ (− 4t)]; [2t; − 4]|= [2t^{2} − 4t + 2; − 4t^{2} + 8t − 4]×]

- [MATH: [2t + 1; − 4t]] [MATH: \text{is}] a solution of the system. Indeed:
[MATH: [(2t + 1)^{′}; (− 4t)^{′}]|= [2|1; − 4|− 2][2t + 1; − 4t]; [2; − 4]|= [2 ⋅ (2t + 1) + 1 ⋅ (− 4t); − 4 ⋅ (2t + 1) + (− 2) ⋅ (− 4t)]; [2; − 4]|= [2; − 4]✓]
- [MATH: [t; 1 − 2t]] [MATH: \text{is}] a solution of the system. Indeed:
[MATH: [(t)^{′}; (1 − 2t)^{′}]|= [2|1; − 4|− 2][t; 1 − 2t]; [1; − 2]|= [2 ⋅ t + 1 ⋅ (1 − 2t); − 4 ⋅ t + (− 2) ⋅ (1 − 2t)]; [1; − 2]|= [1; − 2]✓]

Now, consider the set of solutions [MATH: \big\{ \mathbf{b},\mathbf{c} \big\}.] Its Wronskian is

[MATH: W(b, c)|=|2t + 1|t; − 4t|1 − 2t|; = (2t + 1) ⋅ (1 − 2t) − t ⋅ (− 4t); = (2t + 1)(1 − 2t) + 4t^{2}; = 1]

which is nonzero for at least one [MATH: t \in \mathbb R.] Thus, since [MATH: \mathbf b] and [MATH: \mathbf c] are both solutions of the same linear system, and their Wronskian is nonzero for at least one [MATH: t\in\mathbb R,] [MATH: \big\{ \mathbf{b},\mathbf{c} \big\}] is a set of fundamental solutions of the system.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The Wronskian [MATH: W(\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2)] of two vector-valued functions
[MATH: [x_{11}(t); x_{21}(t)]]
is defined as
[MATH: |x_{11}(t)|x_{12}(t); x_{21}(t)|x_{22}(t)|]

Content:
Analogous to scalar ordinary differential equations (ODEs), the Wronskian of vector-valued functions can be used to determine linear dependency. In particular:

Content:
> - If the Wronskian is not identically zero, then [MATH: \mathbf{x}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{x}_2] are linearly independent.
> - If the Wronskian is identically zero, and it's known that [MATH: \mathbf{x}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{x}_2] are solutions to the same system of linear ODEs, then [MATH: \mathbf{x}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{x}_2] are linearly dependent.

Content:
Let's see some concrete examples.

---

Item 2 — Example: Calculating the Wronskian of Two Vector-Valued Functions

Example Prompt:
[MATH: [t^{3}; 2]]
Find the Wronskian [MATH: W(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2)] of the above vector-valued functions.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The Wronskian [MATH: W(\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2)] of two vector-valued functions
[MATH: [x_{11}(t); x_{21}(t)]]
is defined as
[MATH: |x_{11}(t)|x_{12}(t); x_{21}(t)|x_{22}(t)|]

Therefore, our Wronskian is

[MATH: W(x_{1}, x_{2})|=|t^{3}|t^{3} − 5; 2|4|; = t^{3} ⋅ 4 − (t^{3} − 5) ⋅ 2; = 4t^{3} − 2t^{3} + 10; = 2t^{3} + 10.]

Item 5 — Example: Identifying Linearly Independent Vector-Valued Functions

Example Prompt:
[MATH: [− 4e^{2t}; e^{2t}]]
Consider the vector-valued functions [MATH: \mathbf{x}_1(t)] and [MATH: \mathbf{x}_2(t)] above. Given that [MATH: \mathbf x_1] and [MATH: \mathbf x_2] are solutions of the same system of linear ODEs, compute the Wronskian is [MATH: W(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2)] and determine if the set [MATH: \left\{ \mathbf{x}_1(t), \mathbf{x}_2(t) \right\}] is linearly dependent on [MATH: \mathbb R.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The Wronskian [MATH: W(\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2)] of two vector-valued functions
[MATH: [x_{11}(t); x_{21}(t)]]
is defined as
[MATH: |x_{11}(t)|x_{12}(t); x_{21}(t)|x_{22}(t)|]

Note the following:

- If the Wronskian is not identically zero, then [MATH: \mathbf{x}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{x}_2] are linearly independent.
- If the Wronskian is identically zero, and it's known that [MATH: \mathbf{x}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{x}_2] are solutions to the same system of linear ODEs, then [MATH: \mathbf{x}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{x}_2] are linearly dependent.

In our case, our Wronskian is given by

[MATH: W(x_{1}, x_{2})|=|− 4e^{2t}|e^{t}; e^{2t}|2e^{t}|; = (− 4e^{2t}) ⋅ (2e^{t}) − e^{t} ⋅ (e^{2t}); = − 8e^{3t} − e^{3t}; = − 9e^{3t}]

which is nonzero for at least one [MATH: t\in \mathbb R.]

Therefore, the set [MATH: \left\{ \mathbf{x}_1(t), \mathbf{x}_2(t) \right\}] is linearly independent on [MATH: \mathbb R.]

Item 8 — Tutorial: Fundamental Sets of Solutions for Systems of Linear ODEs

Content:
A pair of solutions [MATH: \mathbf{x}_1(t)] and [MATH: \mathbf{x}_2(t)] to a [MATH: 2\times 2] homogeneous linear system
[MATH: \mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)]
is called a fundamental set of solutions on an interval if the solutions are linearly independent on that interval.

Content:
A practical test for determining whether a pair of functions forms a fundamental set of solutions is to use the Wronskian:

Content:
> If [MATH: \mathbf{x}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{x}_2] are solutions to the system and
> [MATH: W(\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2) \neq 0]
> for at least one [MATH: t_0] in the interval, then they form a fundamental set of solutions on that interval.

Content:
This definition generalizes to any [MATH: n\times n] homogeneous linear system [MATH: \mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t).] A set of solutions
[MATH: \mathbf{x}_1(t),\ \mathbf{x}_2(t),\ \ldots,\ \mathbf{x}_n(t)]
is a fundamental set of solutions on an interval if the solutions are linearly independent on that interval.

Content:
The same Wronskian idea applies: compute the determinant of the [MATH: n\times n] matrix whose columns are [MATH: \mathbf{x}_1(t),\ldots,\mathbf{x}_n(t).] If it is nonzero at some [MATH: t_0] in the interval, then the solutions form a fundamental set on that interval.

Content:
Next, we will look at a concrete example applying this test.

---
